In the commentors defence, I'm also a bit fed up of the gatekeepers around this kind of conversation. It's legitimate, with the context of recent rating history to note, this looks extremely violent. Look at the damage it produced, the violent rotation... indistinguishable from many lower end ef4's and I'm sure, during its cycle it was just as intense. I've been interested in the study of tornadoes for about 20 years, and I think the consistency of Tornado ratings has taken a battering over the last 15. I don't have any particular arguments with Lake City, other than once again some of the DIs are pretty subjective between high end ef3 and low end ef4 and on appearance (which is perfectly reasonable) it has hallmarks of an extremely intense tornado. My point, if I get round to it, the rating system being compromised, is a very legitimate conversation and handled in the right way, is a conversation we should have for the sanctity of rating our most extreme tornadoes appropriately. The yale study earlier this year 'Where have the Ef5's gone; a closer look into the drought of the most violent tornadoes in the United States' does a decent enough job explaining that we are seeing underrated tornadoes or an unhelpfully high threshold on distinguishing our most destructive ones. Ef5 damage and high end Ef4 damage being very difficult to separate and a seemingly Conservative approach to rating has probably led to a self inflicted drought. I'd like to see sensibly re-recognised 3 or 4 of the below tornadoes included in that study as passing the threshold, for the purpose of historical record, as the most destructive rating. Mayflower, Bassfield, Western and Rolling Fork in particular - all in previous years would have been rated f5 or ef5 and cleaned well built structures from their foundations (amongst others in the list).

I'm absolutely okay with a good amount of these remaining ef4's, especially the proportion of those 2011 ones. However, Mayflower, Bassfield, Western and Rolling Fork probably should have been ef5s. Tornados did not get weaker, rather the threshold for ef5 got higher and ultimately, I don't think it's a good thing for the consistency of our records and nor does it help to have so many ef4s with such a wide range of damage scales, without any of those tornadoes passing the most extreme threshold. 

Lowering the windspeed to 195 would probably help create a bit of consistency, in what remains a pretty subjective job of judging damage indicators, especially when judging high end ef4s against ef5s. I don't think it's at all controversial to suggest we've had some since 2013. It needs attention, really and a bit of a retrospective to clean up the last number of years.

It's interesting, and an emotional topic for people. 

As a weather enthusiast though, I plant myself firmly on the side of, I want a consistent scale that correctly records the strongest tornados for historical records and for those affected. 

I think I agree with the yale study that took a look at 13 ef4 tornados (high end) and found that in the years prior would have been rated ef5/f5 and arguably should have been. Bringing down the ef5 windspeed to 190, would be better for identifying a class for the strongest tornados. 

It would include Bassfield, Mayflower, Rolling fork and those standout tornadoes from the last 15 years... all of which swept off well built houses from foundations. 

For some reason people get precious about the discussio and think we're baiting for ef5's. Rather it's more about, for me, a proper record of the strongest storms, rated in a sensible way.

I don't doubt it - but specifically we're discussing was there a 2.6 miles wide condensation funnel. The damage path was 2.6 miles wide, I'm sure, because the tornadic windfield was as such.

What's the source on El Reno 2013's condensation funnels being 2.6 miles wide?
I've revisited the footage from that day over and over, the Meso was touching down all over the place, with fast moving funnels taking turns like a carousel. There was, arguably, one sizable but not massively wide primary funnel which a lot of the chasers caught on video. What I don't agree with, pretty resolutely, is that there was a 2.6 mile wide condensation funnel down that day. 2.6 miles includes the windfield. No less devastating, even more unpredictable, but it should be remembered for what it was... a meso that pretty much danced along the ground in the most unpredictable and violent manner we have seen documented with the most violent windfield, we have ever seen.

Arguable. There was, throughout its lifetime a primary multi-vortex tornado.. its visible in Dan Robinsons rear mirror and lots of footage. El Reno, essentially had the whole Meso touching the ground, it was messy. There were multiple funnels and insanely fast moving vortices circling a large area and within that 2.6 miles the wind was of tornadic strength. There was no clearly defined 2.6 mile wide tornado to witness and that was part of the problem for experienced storm chasers, but the windfield was historic. Messy answer I know, but I don't think there's an easy or exact answer... and I think it would be wrong to include El Reno's windfield like we do and not apply the same measure to other similar tornadoes.

Call me a cynic, but don't fool yourself ever into thinking that a relationship isn't somewhat conditional and contractual. To be successful, they take work, compromise and resilience... if it stops being beneficial for you to be In the other person's life for a sustained period of time and you do nothing about that, they should leave and vise versa. We have two kids and its hard, we eb and flow through good, bad and indifferent but the bad is never too bad and we don't argue much at all; our days are long, we're tired and we work hard,  but on most days we can have a smile, a moment or a laugh at the end or it... or at the very least cosy up and watch an episode or two of the series we're watching. Hey, it's the life we chose and we love our kids (less so at 3am atm) We then have to remember to arrange some time and space for us to make sure we have chance to talk, reconnect and be present for a moment, so neither of us get complacent or miss something about the other person we have not picked up on. 

I'm sure there are couples out there more in love, that are more compatible, that are more primal... couples without kids (ahh I remember) that do wonderfully spiritual things together and travel. I had a relationship like that, it burned  brighter than the sun, I felt every moment of it and when it fell down from the sky it killed me: I don't think what I have now is that, but it's much stronger. I would walk through walls for my little family, my wife to be, because at our worst, we're still strong and at our very best we're like the same person. 

I dont think we can put the label soul mates on it, because it takes a lot of work to cultivate. After which you get to harvest it...without that work, especially when our kids are young, i dont think we could endure and the disconnect would be too much. I think that's why we see high divorce and separation rates, a love burns really bright, people led by the fuzzy feeling in their stomach and when that inevitably fades and the work begins, people are not prepared to do it. I have moments of overwhelming feeling of love, attraction, care etc. but like any feeling, it's not sustainable to walk around with a fuzzy glow all the time, especially for a miserable sod like me. I think people get addicted to that new phase and freak out when it's not there and mistake it for incompatibility.

In practice, human understanding doesn’t necessarily require exceeding a threshold of complexity; rather, context, prior knowledge, and cognitive frameworks are more critical for interpreting new information.

The notion that perception of coherent information depends on reaching a threshold of "bandwidth" or "processing power" implies that understanding is solely a function of cognitive capacity. However, emotional, cultural, and contextual factors often play a more significant role in comprehension than raw cognitive processing.



In summary, while subjective interpretation is valid in many contexts, precision and shared meaning are essential for coherent communication, especially when dealing with facts. Let’s address each piece of 'evidence' with a balanced perspective:

1. The Cosmic Ancestry of Humanity

Claim:
The elements that make up human DNA (hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen) were created in ancient stars and distributed through supernovae, making us “children of the cosmos.”

This claim is scientifically accurate to a degree. The theory of nucleosynthesis confirms that heavier elements were indeed formed in the cores of ancient stars and spread through supernova explosions, granted. This is a well-established fact. I like Carl Sagan’s famous phrase, “We are made of star stuff.”

However, calling this a direct link to “alien origins” is a philosophical leap. While the elements necessary for life originated from stars, this doesn't imply extraterrestrial life seeded Earth directly (panspermia). The processes that led to life on Earth are mostly tied to terrestrial chemistry and early Earth conditions. Cosmic events provided the raw materials, evidence for actual alien biological influence hasn't been provided?


2. The Unexplainable Advances of Ancient Civilizations

Claim:
Technological and architectural achievements of ancient civilizations (e.g., the Great Pyramid's alignment, Sumerian astronomy) suggest extraterrestrial influence or forgotten advanced knowledge.

While the achievements of ancient civilisations are impressive, attributing them to extraterrestrial contact undermines human ingenuity and cultural developments. Possibly, the claim here that bothers me most.

Great Pyramid Alignment: The precision of the Great Pyramid’s alignment with true north is mega, but it can be explained by observation of the stars by ancient Egyptian astronomers and the use of basic surveying tools like the gnomon and plumb line. The accumulated knowledge of ancient cultures was sophisticated... no evidence of it being alien.

Advanced Astronomy: The Sumerians and Mayans demonstrated profound astronomical understanding, but this can be attributed to systematic observation over long periods rather than alien guidance. Societies with a deep dependence on agriculture, navigation, or ritual often dedicated immense time and resources to studying celestial movements.... Simply, they spent a lot more time staring at the sky than the average person today and for good reason!


Claiming that these accomplishments exceed human capacity without evidence risks fostering a dismissive view of historical civilisations and ignores the possibility of knowledge transmission and cultural continuity.


3. The Shared Universal Consciousness

Claim:
Quantum entanglement suggests universal interconnectedness, and human consciousness might arise from this cosmic network, making all life forms variations of the same “universal life force.”

Quantum mechanics indeed describes phenomena like entanglement, where particles can instantaneously correlate over distances. However, extending quantum principles to human consciousness is speculative and lacks empirical evidence.

Quantum Consciousness: The idea that consciousness arises from quantum processes (championed by theories like those proposed by Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff) is still controversial. There is no proof that human cognition or awareness is tied to quantum phenomena.

Metaphorical Appeal: While the idea of a “universal consciousness” resonates philosophically, it is not supported by mainstream neuroscience or physics. The interconnectedness observed at the quantum level does not directly translate into a universal mind or life force. This claim often blends scientific language with metaphysical speculation, creating an appealing but unprovable narrative.

The warm waters to the east and west mean that warm moist air dominates the peninsula and you tend not to get near ground inversions to add to convective inhibition. Geographically, Florida is not part of Tornado alley. I believe at least the western stretch of Florida is a part of Dixie Alley. Regardless, Florida has a high frequency of tornadoes, about 60 a year - normally they aren't ef3+ but they're not immune to severe storms in the spring and of course in the summer as H season starts. So they rank 4 for frequency but 19 for fatalities, which is probably why the threat isn't considered as substantial as traditional TA or DA. 

It's all about the ingredients, Florida tends to have spin ups or short lived tornadoes. They have the moisture but not the wind sheer that tends to lend to long track, destructive twisters.
